title: Kernel matchmaking for fragmented KV and prefill surge controller
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary:
We see tail decode latency spikes during short, bursty workloads when fragmented KV pages cause kernel mismatch and expensive prefill stalls. This ticket implements a kernel-matchmaking layer that picks compatible kernel variants for a request given the current KV fragmentation footprint, plus a prefill surge controller that hedges between partial prefill, kernel substitution, and deferred-prefill to keep p95/p99 latency within SLOs while preserving cache reuse.

Background / motivation:
- Observed patterns: small-stepped chat sessions frequently access scattered KV fragments, leading to repeated kernel-context switches and decode stalls.
- Current runtime routes to the highest-throughput kernel without considering fragment layout or prefill costs, causing costly evictions and reclaims under burst load.
- Customers run mixed workloads (interactive + background) and care about predictable latency; bursts increase token cost due to repeated prefill work.

Goals and success metrics:
- Reduce p95 decode latency for 0.1–5s inter-token arrival bursts by 20–30%.
- Reduce redundant prefill work (prefill byte-rate) by at least 15% on sampled chat workloads.
- Keep overall token throughput within 5% of baseline and avoid regressions on long-context generative jobs.
- Instrumentation: p50/p95/p99 decode latency, prefill-miss-rate, kernel-switch-count-per-request, avg fragment contiguity, eviction-churn, tenant fairness score.

Design overview:
1) Kernel matchmaking service (in-runtime):
   - Input: candidate kernels, request sequence-length profile, KV fragment map for relevant shards/pages, historical kernel residency/latency stats.
   - Scoring: cost = kernel_switch_overhead + estimated_prefill_cost - expected_reuse_benefit. Scores computed cheaply using cached heuristics (no blocking RPCs).
   - Output: ordered kernel candidate list with attached prefill strategy tag (full, partial, deferred).

2) Prefill surge controller:
   - Detects bursty traffic via sliding-window arrival rate and prefill queue length.
   - Hedge strategies: (A) partial-prefill (hot-prefix only), (B) kernel-substitution to a kernel tolerant of fragmented pages, (C) deferred-prefill with background warmup.
   - Admission policy chooses conservative strategy under capacity pressure and aggressive strategy when reuse probability high.

3) Fragment-aware kernel adapters:
   - Kernel variants expose capabilities: contiguous-only, sparse-accept, zero-copy-overlay. Matchmaking prefers kernels that minimize copy/prefill cost for current fragmentation signature.

4) Page-transfer coordination for reuse:
   - When prefill must reconstruct a contiguous view from fragments, perform lightweight page-transfer within the shard (non-blocking) and annotate pages with "recently-stitched" TTL to bias reuse.

Trade-offs considered:
- Memory amplification vs latency: stitching fragments increases transient memory; limit with budgeted transfers and TTLs.
- Heuristic complexity vs stability: start with simple additive scoring to avoid oscillations.
- Tenant fairness: ensure surge controller enforces per-tenant thresholds to prevent noisy-neighbor stealing.

Implementation plan / milestones:
- Spike (1 week): synthetic microbench to validate scoring heuristics; implement offline scorer prototype and run replay of 24h traffic sample.
- Alpha (2 weeks): implement kernel-matchmaker (read-only heuristics), wire in a single kernel-substitution path and partial-prefill policy behind runtime flag. Add metrics.
- Canary (2 weeks): staged rollout to 5% of serving fleet with canary traffic slice (interactive-heavy) + automatic rollback on latency regressions.
- Beta (2 weeks): expand to 30% with more kernel variants and page-transfer coordination.
- Postmortem & tuning (1 week): refine heuristics and finalize rollout.

Experiments & benchmarks planned:
- Replay synthetic bursts at 0.1s, 0.5s, 1s inter-arrival to measure prefill cost and kernel-switch counts.
- Real-traffic shadow run for 48h to capture eviction churn and fragment contiguity improvement.
- AB test measuring p95 latency and token-cost per session.

Observability / telemetry additions:
- new metrics: runtime.kernel_candidate_score, runtime.prefill_strategy_chosen, runtime.kernel_switch_latency, runtime.fragment_contiguity_ratio, runtime.stitched_pages_count.
- Logs: structured decision logs for a sampled subset of requests (reason codes, scores, chosen strategy).

Rollout plan / safety knobs:
- Feature flag gating (global + per-cluster + tenant override).
- CPU/memory soft-limits for page transfers; abort if >X% memory usage.
- Canary thresholds: if p95 latency increases >10% or eviction-churn increases >25% during canary, auto-rollback.

Open questions / risks:
- How to weight long-term reuse vs immediate latency for multitenant fairness? (Need policy discussion with product/security).
- Is partial-prefill good enough for very high-fragmentation models where copying is expensive? May require kernel-level sparse-acceleration.
- Risk of oscillation when matchmaking repeatedly flips kernels; mitigations: sticky-decisions TTL and dampening.

Next steps / action items:
- Aisha: run replay spike with three candidate scoring weight sets and post results to this ticket (due 2025-02-21).
- Marcus: prototype kernel substitution interface and add a lightweight capability descriptor to kernel registration (due 2025-02-28).
- QA: prepare canary harness and SLA gating tests (due 2025-03-10).
